questions.q: According to this lesson's decision process, what should you try first when combining two tables in Tableau?
options: A relationship — it's the default: no fan-out risk, and it auto-aggregates per worksheet
A blend — it's the safest option in every case
A join — it should always be your first choice since it matches SQL
There is no recommended order; all three are equally good starting points
questions.explain: Relationships are the recommended default: flexible, context-aware, and free of the fan-out risk a mismatched-grain join can cause.

questions.q: When should you drop from a relationship down to a real join?
options: When you need something a relationship can't express — a non-equality condition, an intentional row-duplication setup, or a single flat physical table for performance
Whenever the two tables come from the same Excel workbook
Every time you're combining more than two tables
Joins should never be used if a relationship is available
questions.explain: Joins earn their place when a relationship's more flexible, deferred combination can't do what you need — non-equality conditions, deliberate duplication, or single-table performance needs.

questions.q: When is blending your only real option, according to this lesson?
options: When one source is a published Tableau data source, the connectors can't support a cross-database join, or the linking field needs to vary sheet by sheet
Whenever both sources are Excel files
Whenever you need row-level analysis across two sources
Blending should always be preferred over relationships
questions.explain: Blending is the fallback specifically for cases relationships and joins structurally can't handle: published sources, incompatible connectors, or per-sheet linking flexibility.

questions.q: Which of the three techniques carries a fan-out (row-duplication) risk if the two tables have mismatched granularity?
options: A join — because rows combine immediately at the row level, like a SQL JOIN
A relationship — because it always duplicates rows immediately
A blend — because it combines rows at the row level before aggregating
None of the three ever risk fan-out
questions.explain: A join combines immediately at the row level, so mismatched grains can multiply rows (Lesson 50). Relationships auto-aggregate per worksheet, and blends aggregate each source independently — neither risks the same fan-out.

questions.q: In this lesson's SQL translation, what is a Tableau relationship closest to?
options: Deferring the join decision until query time, letting Tableau decide based on which columns a worksheet actually selects — something plain SQL doesn't really have an equivalent for
An exact match for SQL's JOIN keyword
A stored procedure
A SQL view that's refreshed nightly
questions.explain: Unlike a join (which behaves exactly like SQL's JOIN), a relationship's context-aware, per-worksheet aggregation doesn't map cleanly onto a single SQL construct.
